items.title: Nvidia and the World Without Jensen
items.content:
Jensen Huang is no longer the CEO of Nvidia . Nvidia’s board was investigating Jensen’s conduct and weighing his future at the company he founded, and clearly the conduct issue is real; it is ethically problematic to have relationships with a customer who is a Chinese CCP asset and with multiple subordinates.
 Additionally, we believe there is more at play with his resignatiom after only four days. We believe it is directly tied to the vast smuggling of GPUs. Our Accelerator Model tracks every AI chip’s production and destination, and our data shows more than 1.5GW of Nvidia chips, which are restricted, still ultimately ended up in China. This figure doesn’t even include chips that Nvidia created to circumvent US rules, a story we originally broke .
 We believe the US intelligence community is a large part of the push to get Jensen out of Nvidia. Specifically, we believe it is likely that RASA or similar legislation, which has already passed the house, will move forward. AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone. We are strong believers in some restrictions, but poorly shaped ones are damaging to US interests.
 This sort of legislation will have consequences, and we don’t think politicians are thinking them through.
 Here are the clear benefits of the current regime where Chinese labs are able to access GPUs remotely, and NOT in China:
 Profits flow to American companies.
 The US can monitor what Chinese labs are doing.
 The US can cut off their access to the GPUs through politics or by force almost instantly, if they choose.
 American companies such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Supermicro, and Dell all depend on Chinese companies in their supply chain.
 American companies such as NVIDIA and AMD employ Chinese engineers (who live in China, to be clear) to develop hardware and low-level software for their GPU systems. Without these engineers, we are certain that the user experience for these GPUs would be materially worse than it is today.
 American companies, especially the entire startup ecosystem benefit from the open source research that Chinese companies, students and independent researchers publish using these GPUs today.
 China is (even slightly) less motivated to use their domestic accelerators.
 Innovations from China flow globally through open innovations of wide expert parallelism, OSS kernel libraries: MSA, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, etc.
 With that said we do believe in some AI restrictions to China, but those are more shaped like the MATCH Act then RASA. Biden style diffusion rules make the most sense.
 Maybe biggest of all: open source is under attack . It’s an open secret that Nvidia works directly with the Chinese labs on open source and helping them optimize GPUs and models. These labs utilize Blackwell GPUs, which Nvidia knows. The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning.
 But the question that matters for shareholders (and the AI supply chain) is a different one: what is Nvidia without Jensen?
 Our view is that the company was never built for him not to be there. He was at the helm for 33 years, and even though the board pressured him out (or he “resigned”) Nvidia would still be materially better off with him there instead of gone. The company was uniquely built to suit the man himself. The company without the man might be an entirely different beast. SpaceX and Tesla don't function without Elon, Nvidia doesn't function without Jensen.
 One King, 60 Direct Reports Nvidia’s corporate structure is odd for a company of its size and scale. Jensen has roughly 60 direct reports, according to his public statements. He has said that CEOs should have the most direct reports because those people require the least amount of management and that he doesn’t have one-on-one meetings with them.
 But few of them can do things without Jensen. The company is run like a kingdom with one king, with everyone else, regardless of seniority, a peon doing his bidding. Jensen has said that it doesn’t matter who reports to who as their title isn’t related to how important their job is, and it’s one of the reasons why Nvidia is the “smallest large company in the word” and has so much fewer employees – about 42,000 – despite its big market cap. At Nvidia, there is less politics as a result. Jensen has said this flat network empowers employees and allows the company to adapt more quickly because its technology is also moving so quickly.
 This is one of the reasons Nvidia moves fast. Once Jensen set a direction, everyone moved on it together. Former employees have told us that product development and engineering often happen until the last minute so the company can change its mind if it needs to. For example, the GB200 design came together a lot closer to the product cycle than probably anyone would have liked, one former executive told us. Jensen has said he wishes he could keep the company in startup mode forever.
 The cost of that structure, however, is that Nvidia doesn’t have a deep bench of successors. Look at Nvidia’s website: only five others, two of whom are legal and finance executives, are featured prominently among his reports. Most of his direct reports aren’t trained for the spotlight and are actively discouraged from seeking it. Few leave to become CEOs of other major companies, with Rene Haas at Arm the rare exception. Few at Nvidia get the chance to shine externally because Jensen makes all the big decisions. But much of Nvidia’s executive team doesn’t mind because heavy is the head that wears the crown, and many are happy to stay until retirement age because they’re well paid, treated well, and believe in the mission and their leader.
 No One Wants the Job Colette Kress has been named interim CEO, but Nvidia is looking for a permanent CEO. That cannot be someone with finance background. The obvious internal names being floated to succeed Jensen on the technical side are Ian Buck and Jonah Alben. Buck, who created CUDA out of his doctoral research at Stanford, joined Nvidia in 2004 and now runs the datacenter business as vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He is often placed in charge of things while Jensen travels and frequently speaks at conferences.
 Alben, who has been at Nvidia since 1997, is senior vice president of GPU engineering and oversees the design of the company’s GPUs. But realistically, no one person can run it all. We don’t think Buck is capable of running the technical hardware engineering side of the house. Alben and others on his team have technical autonomy, but even he doesn’t control the entire chip side, where other senior leaders who handle many major technical and business divisions also report directly to Jensen. Both are amazing but likely not able to exert the supply chain mastery Jensen has.
 There is also the question of whether anyone wants to do the job of CEO. An executive told us earlier this year that “Ian would rather die than succeed Jensen and wouldn’t want that job. Jonah is more respected and people say he could, but again, no one would really want that job.” Circumstances, though, have obviously changed. Kress is the interim CEO, but wrangling more than 60 VPs to a cohesive vision of the company takes a certain kind of person, and otherwise the firm’s direction risks dissolving into noise.
 Founder Bets Do Not Survive Professional Managers Jensen is one of the last old-school tech founders, of the same generation as Elon Musk and a bit older than Mark Zuckerberg. The other companies that came up alongside Nvidia have all transitioned to professional managers, including AMD, Google, Microsoft, Apple and Amazon.
 Nvidia’s success relies on big bets that can take years, if not a decade, to pay off. A founder with the full support of the board can take those risks without worrying about a revolt. CUDA lost money for years while Wall Street analysts kept questioning it, but Jensen held steady and the bet paid off enormously. As one former employee put it: “Jensen put the whole company behind programmable shaders, CUDA and tensor cores despite a lot of opposition to spending transistors on them when use was limited.”
 Omniverse and autonomous driving are the new bets within Nvidia. Internally, Jensen calls them “zero billion dollar bets,” former employees tell us. They make no money today, but he sees them as just as big as CUDA. He also built the Shield TV consumer entertainment box and the DGX Cloud service on the idea that Nvidia needs to understand its customers to design better products, even if those two businesses made little or no money and were ultimately cast aside.
 An Nvidia successor who isn’t the founder, no matter how long they have been at the company, answers to the board and shareholders in a different way. Long-term bets and convictions of this kind become much less likely, and one of the biggest issues is Jensen’s legendary kingmaking and dealmaking, which is going to be hard to replicate.
 Customers Bought Jensen, Not Just GPUs Jensen was the chief decider on chip allocation to the hyperscalers and everyone else. Customers are always jockeying for allocation and fighting for Nvidia’s attention, and more and more of Nvidia’s deals require extensive Nvidia support. As we wrote in July , Nvidia has a choice over whether to allocate more capacity to hyperscalers, neoclouds or neoclouds on its backstop program, where it credit-supports the cluster and takes a share of the cloud revenue. This central bank of Nvidia was backed by the full faith and credit of Jensen. The next CEO is unlikely to be able to make the bold bets Jensen did.
 Nvidia likes to decide based on what’s feasible, but much of it comes down to what makes strategic sense. It doesn’t always make strategic sense to skip the hyperscalers, or to work with them and treat them preferentially. Many of these customers now need reassurances that they will continue to be supported by Nvidia through financial guarantees or allocation. Nvidia disclosed $530B of gross off-balance-sheet guarantees as of its fiscal second quarter, up from $184B the prior quarter, including $36B of take-or-pay floors under neocloud capacity, and it holds a $99B equity book.
 Many customers also want a deal with Jensen for reasons that go beyond the numbers. Neoclouds around the world raised their money because Jensen backed them, not because they compared chips and chose Nvidia. Nvidia’s backstops let neoclouds and neolabs raise money without the hyperscalers: it sells GPUs at full margin on day one, then floors the buyer’s revenue, guarantees the buyer’s landlord or signs the lease itself, so that operators without an investment-grade rating can borrow at investment-grade pricing. If the Jensen put is not there, there might be a large contraction in this ecosystem.
 The Supply Chain Stranglehold Loosens Nvidia has a stranglehold on its suppliers. If competitors had access to supply, they would ship much higher volume. They can’t get it because Jensen has personally locked up memory in South Korea and chips in Taiwan. As we wrote in The Great AI Silicon Shortage , Nvidia has locked in most of the supply for logic wafers, memory and various other necessary components, and Jensen’s 2025 trip to Korea was to secure memory supply, before other executives quite realized how in shortage memory was. Our industry clients thought our forecasts for 2026 were too aggressive, but then they realized we were right . Nvidia’s supply and capacity commitments jumped from $119B to $279B in a single quarter, primarily for memory.
 That stranglehold is personal. Jensen was the one who won these deals, CEO to CEO, with the major supply chain companies around the world. In Korea, we estimate SK Hynix’s 2027 HBM4 pricing could range from roughly $3.0 to $3.3 per Gb for Nvidia versus $3.7 to $4.1 per Gb for other Tier 1 customers including AMD, Broadcom, Amazon and Google, and we believe there is an implicit understanding that Nvidia gives SK Group priority GPU allocation in return. Without him, these firms will no longer prioritize Nvidia to the same degree, and capacity will be easier for others to acquire. We think it’s likely that in 2028 more than 70% of total capacity could be non-Nvidia. 
 What’s more, beyond strangling the supply, Jensen’s vision is what pushed the supply chain in Taiwan to invest harder and believe more in this buildout than anyone else. Jensen’s legendary supply chain dinners and commitments are what pushed suppliers in Taiwan to deliver on technologically and logistically aggressive plans.
 The AI Industry Loses Its Open Source Spokesman Without Jensen, the AI industry loses its chief spokesman. He was everywhere, speaking on AI as its chief proponent. He was the face of AI, and no one can replace that.
 Jensen also set Nvidia’s China policy and led its push for open source AI models, which give countries, enterprises and neoclouds a reason to buy GPUs beyond the handful of frontier labs, who are now building their own chips.
 As we wrote in September , no one needs open source AI more than Nvidia: it is on track for a world where it has only two real customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, or seven including the hyperscalers, and all seven except SpaceX are trying to build their own XPUs to cannibalize Nvidia’s margins. AI models and applications are the complements to its GPUs.
 It is an open secret that Chinese frontier labs use Blackwell GPUs & NVIDIA DevTech collaborates closely with the Chinese frontier labs & learns a lot from their end users, which results in innovations to the CUDA ecosystem like wide expert parallelism, DeepGEMM, DeepEP etc. These then spread to the western open source community and startups. These startups are massively negatively impacted by the departure.
 Without Jensen being the spokesperson and offering financial and engineering help for open models, Chinese labs may not be able to open source kernel libraries like MiniMax MSA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, Moonshot’s FlashKDA, which are clearly targeted at NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Many production engines used widely across the world like SGLang & vLLM use these innovations from Chinese labs. Chinese labs may have to go back to straight up denying that they have any NVIDIA GPUs and keep their NVIDIA software internal only instead of open sourcing Blackwell software.
 This is fundamentally bad that innovations from China won’t be shared across the NVIDIA ecosystem & the general ML ecosystem anymore. It is positive for closed AI labs but bad for startups.
 A manager lead company could depriortize underperforming Nemotron , With many models going closed source at the frontier labs in the U.S., Nvidia was single-handedly propping up the other American open source models with its efforts by investing in firms like Reflection, Thinking Machines, Poolside, and the Hugging Face acquisition.
 Nvidia was the one pushing continuous engagement with China, on the argument that China should use and rely on American technology. As we wrote last year , after the U.S. government banned the H20 from going into China and then indicated Nvidia would be granted a license to export it, the U.S. needs to balance having China on the U.S. AI stack and slowing the development of its own, while also limiting the quality and volumes shipped into China. Now, what if he was pushing it from a compromised place? That is up to the investigation to figure out. Clearly the China hawks are winning, so we have to ask a bit of an odd question. Why now?
 Why Now Does Jensen’s Personal Life Come to Light? We aren’t ones for conspiracy theories, but a few events around the same time seem to create a narrative that is hard to ignore. The intelligence community had much to gain. The second New York Times story on the topic explicitly states (five times) that the basis for its reporting is the U.S. intelligence community. Trump, Rubio and Lutnick have known about all of this since before their trip to China in May. What’s more is that there is reporting that Lutnick stalled the Chinese chip crackdown . Something has shifted in that relationship, and now the wind is blowing in the other direction.
 We actually don’t believe Alice Huang is a spy in the traditional sense. She is a well connected business woman. She like any other well connected business person in China, has contact with the CCP. 
 Our Accelerator Model has tracked over 1.5GW of Nvidia GPUs that shouldn’t be in China, The Department of Commerce now also finally believes that there is more than 1.5GW of NVIDIA chips in China that shouldn’t be there. Now, with the midterms swinging the Democrat’s way, someone has decided it is time to put the hammer down both to stop the willing circumvention of the existing export controls and to expand them to cut off China’s access to frontier chips once and for all.
 To be clear, the Trump administration is split on the issue, but Trump was giving Lutnick cover. Trump is no longer providing that cover. What’s more, there is a critical bill called the Remote Access Security Act (“RASA”) that has passed the House that has yet to receive a vote in the Senate, and that vote is happening right now.
 RASA Up for a Vote RASA passed the House 369-22 on Jan. 12. It passed on a motion to suspend the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority. The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved it 51-0 in April 2025. Though it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, it hasn’t yet received a vote. We know that NVIDIA and Oracle have been lobbying against it, hard .
 Of course, RASA isn’t the only way that the U.S. government can stop Chinese companies from accessing GPUs remotely. But RASA is the bill that is the hot topic of discussion in Washington right now. It is clearly popular, having already passed the House, and the substantive portions of the bill seem downright obvious to people. Why allow Chinese companies to access GPUs remotely that they aren’t allowed to import?
 For what it’s worth, we are aware of neoclouds in Asia, Australia, the Middle East, Nordics, Europe, Canada and even the U.S. that are actively selling capacity to Chinese companies. All of them would be impacted by this bill. This is another global export control bill, and one with far-reaching implications. Jensen, and likely Lutnick, did not want this to happen.
 So let’s go against the popular narrative and explore the possibility that despite all of the recent headlines, passing RASA (or something like it) will have unintended consequences . items.title: We Visited China’s Stargate in Inner Mongolia
items.content:
Stargate Abilene has become the symbol of America’s AI buildout. It is a gigawatt-scale campus on the Texas plains built for OpenAI. China has campuses on a similar scale, though few people outside the country have had a look inside. In September, we visited one, and we found the speed, scale, ultra low cost, and deep vertical integration astonishing.
 During the trip, we toured Inner Mongolia, China’s fastest-growing AI datacenter region. It's the “West Texas” of China, but while the Lone Star State faces its highest ever anti-datacenter sentiment, Inner Mongolia is accelerating and faces no such backlash.
 Our main stop was Galaxy, a campus in Ulanqab planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity. 
 Galaxy is about the size of Abilene’s core campus. Its first 120MW phase was delivered within a year at a fifth of US costs. All four phases are built-to-suit for two internet giants. 

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 When we visited, the rest of the campus was still a busy construction site, and the surrounding Chahar High-tech Zone had nearly 30,000 construction workers on site across 22 datacenter projects according to a local report. As we noted in our primer on the China datacenter market , with this much labor available, Chinese datacenters rarely take a fully modular approach, yet construction costs keep falling. We take a closer look at why in this report. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The datacenter is owned by Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator with more than 100GW of wind turbines installed worldwide. It came to datacenters from energy management, a path many others are taking today. Yet it is one of the most vertically integrated players we have ever seen. 
 Beyond running the datacenter, Envision builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply it. Its blade factory sits just across the road from the Galaxy datacenter campus, with finished blades stacked in the yard. 
 Inside the campus, it designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V system, manufactured the battery storage that smooths the load, and co-designed the prefabricated substation.

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 In one 5MW hall, we saw the 800V system at work. Solid-state transformers (SSTs) take 10kV AC from the grid and convert it straight to 800V DC for the racks. This removes the low-voltage transformers, UPS and rectifier stages in between. The same architecture is still on the US roadmap, as we outlined in our 800V DC deep dive .
 In China, datacenters have been running on DC power for almost two decades, from China Telecom’s 240V DC pilots in 2007 to Alibaba’s Panama power system in 2018. Today, roughly a quarter of Chinese datacenters built in the past decade run on DC, while about 97% of US datacenters still use AC UPS. An SST is a natural next step on that path, and we cover the evolution and the pilot in detail later in this report. 

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 On cooling, Galaxy uses a design common in Inner Mongolia. Liquid- and air-cooled servers share one water loop, with no central chiller plant. Nvidia says Vera Rubin can run on 45°C water without chillers, yet most datacenters in the US keep one for air-cooled equipment and for the flexibility to shift between the two. Galaxy drops the central chiller and keeps much of that flexibility, a design that has been running at scale in northern China for years.
 In this report, we use what we saw on the site visit to show how China builds hyperscale datacenters today, with a deep dive on each of the topics above. Many questions still open on the US roadmap find a reference point here. 
 Our next report will take a wider view of Inner Mongolia’s datacenter market. The region has lined up 25GW of announced datacenter projects, including several gigawatt-scale campuses. Many reports picture it as a land of empty datacenter halls. Our data tells a different story. Few have asked what limits datacenter development there. We look at each constraint, from power to land and water. Stay tuned. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model This trip was part of our ongoing fieldwork for the SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model , the China counterpart to our global SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model . 
 It tracks over 1,000 facilities across 70+ operators, with quarterly delivery curves through 2032, a lease signing and delivery tracker, and EDWC hub and cluster analytics. Every project in our report is tracked in the model. 
 Contact sales@semianalysis.com for more information.
 SemiAnalysis is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

 China’s Stargate campus Envision comes to datacenters as a renewable systems integrator. Beyond building wind turbines, it designs, integrates, and manages power systems across the full chain, from generation and storage to computing loads. Its affiliate, Envision AESC, develops and integrates batteries, energy storage systems, and the power electronics and software that link them.
 Inner Mongolia has far more wind than its existing industry and population can use, so policy encourages bringing new demand to where the renewable resources are. In Chifeng, Envision built a 2GW off-grid wind, solar and storage system that feeds a green ammonia plant. The system runs entirely on power electronics, with no synchronous generator. A small pilot datacenter built with Tencent’s modular T-Block units runs on the same system. Galaxy is a larger application of the same idea. 
 This is a pattern we see across China right now. Industrial groups with an edge in energy, construction or electrical equipment are pivoting into AI infrastructure. Project returns are thin, with IRRs squeezed hard, so the reward often comes from elsewhere. For Envision, datacenters create new demand for the power and equipment it already produces. For many listed companies, the draw is the stock market. 
 Of these newcomers, Envision is one of the most ambitious. Its datacenter plans in Inner Mongolia add up to 3GW. Galaxy is the first. Its initial phase was delivered in August 2026, and the full campus is expected to be completed by the end of 2027. 

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The scale of the campus invites comparison with Stargate’s flagship campus in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe began building Abilene in mid-2024 and leased it to Oracle, which runs it for OpenAI. Crusoe describes the eight-building campus as 1.2GW of power, which comes to about 820MW of critical IT capacity, on par with the 800MW planned at Galaxy. That makes Galaxy one of the largest single campuses in China. Our SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model also tracks an expansion phase that Crusoe plans to add, powered behind the meter, which takes the whole Abilene site to 1.5GW of IT capacity. Galaxy also has room to grow. If the wind turbine factory next to the campus is converted, a later expansion phase could take the campus to ~1GW.
 In addition to scale, the two share a starting point. Both are developed by companies with roots in energy, and both were planned around their own power. Abilene draws on the grid and on gas turbines on site, while Galaxy relies largely on wind. 
 What sets Galaxy apart from Abilene, and what draws our attention, is its vertical integration. 
 Own wind for its own load Galaxy’s power comes through a model China calls source-grid-load-storage (”SGLS”). Under this model, a project builds its own wind and/or solar farm, battery storage and datacenter, and links them through a dedicated line instead of the public grid. 
 For hyperscalers, the appeal of an SGLS project is long-term power at a largely fixed cost. Power from wind and solar also counts toward green targets.
 Inner Mongolia holds about 57% of China’s usable wind resources. A wind farm here runs on average about 2,800 full-load hours a year, a capacity factor of roughly 32%. Ulanqab is windier, with a capacity factor of 35–40%. That sets the starting point for how much of an SGLS project’s power can come from wind.
 For Galaxy, Envision aims to supply over 60% of the first two phases’ power use with its own wind farms. Three factors make this possible:
 Siting. Envision chose windy sites, even though they sit about two hours’ drive from the campus. The two wind farms are about 80km apart, which cuts the hours in a year when neither has wind.
 Scale. The wind farms have a combined 420MW of installed capacity, about 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load. With this oversizing, even light-wind hours can still cover much of the load.
 Storage. A 4-hour battery storage system shifts power from windy hours into calm ones. Most SGLS projects add storage too, but Envision makes its own storage systems and runs them on its own software, which we detail in the next section.
 The chart below shows how each factor raises the wind share, using illustrative curves. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 Panel 1 starts with a simple case: 1MW of wind for every 1MW of datacenter load. A good site in Ulanqab produces as much power in a year as running flat out for about 3,500 hours. To keep it simple, the panel shows the farm at full output for 3,500 hours and at zero for the rest of the year. Wind covers 40% of the year’s power.
 Panel 2 shows a more realistic picture. Wind output goes up and down, so the panel sorts every hour of the year from windiest to calmest. The farm is the same size as the load, so it never produces more than the campus uses. All its power gets used, and wind still covers 40%.
 Panel 3 doubles the wind farm. Output in every hour doubles too, so even light-wind hours now cover much of the load, and wind’s share rises to about 55%. The cost shows in the gray area. In windy hours, the farm produces more than the campus can use, and that power must be stored or curtailed.
 Panels 4 and 5 show what can be added on top. A 4-hour battery moves some surplus into the hours after the wind drops, though it cannot help much when the wind stays calm for days. Better matching between wind output and load can push the share even higher. 
 The table at the bottom shows how the result changes with wind quality, the size of the wind farm relative to the load, and how fully the datacenter is used.
 Inside the campus: developer, designer and integrator Beyond pairing energy production with consumption, Envision is also integrated inside the campus, acting as more than a developer and operator. The chart below shows its three roles, in three colors.

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The first is as a manufacturer. Envision designs its own turbines and develops the converters and control software. The battery energy storage systems (BESS) at both the datacenter campus and the wind farm come from its affiliate AESC, which builds every major part in-house, from cells to power conversion and software, so the whole system can be tuned and tested together at the factory before shipping. Most vendors cover only one part of the system (high voltage, low voltage or generators), so getting the parts to work together falls to on-site commissioning, which can take 3–6 months. Envision’s factory pre-configuration has become its core selling point. 
 The second role goes beyond Envision’s traditional business into the datacenter space. For Galaxy, Envision designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V SST system. 
 800V DC is the architecture that Nvidia is pushing for its next generation of high-density racks, as Kyber racks at around 600kW cannot be served efficiently at today’s voltages. In the US, the industry is still early on this path. SSTs that convert medium-voltage AC straight into 800V DC are the final step. Galaxy’s SST pilot is only 5MW, but it already runs 800V DC all the way to the rack at a live hyperscaler site. We discuss this in detail shortly. 
 Lastly, Envision co-designed the prefabricated substation sitting inside the campus. The substation is built and tested as modules in the factory while civil work goes on at the site, then shipped and connected on site. This takes less than 3 months, versus about 6 months for a conventional indoor substation.
 Today, vertical integration on its own does not lead to hyperscaler orders, but two trends suggest it could matter more over time.
 First, access to power is becoming central to datacenter development. In the US, developers bridge the power gap with on-site gas turbines, fuel cells and batteries. In Southeast Asia, governments have been pushing developers to bring their own power this year. Malaysia now requires datacenters to source at least 30% of their power from renewables and encourages on-site generation. In China, approvals increasingly favor projects that pair compute with green power, under the national push for “Compute Power Coordination.” Across different markets, access to energy is becoming part of what a datacenter developer sells.
 Second, the power architecture from the grid connection to the rack is being redesigned. In the US, the industry is moving toward higher-voltage DC power, while battery backup units (BBUs) and BESS are starting to take over the role of UPS. The technology roadmap is not settled yet, but the shift looks set to continue, giving integrated players room to compete differently from traditional developers. 
 These trends have drawn other players onto a similar path. The closest case is the tie-up between VNET, CATL and Zhongheng Electric. 
 VNET is a leading colocation operator, CATL is the world’s largest EV battery maker, and Zhongheng Electric is China’s largest supplier of HVDC power systems for datacenters, working with both Alibaba and ByteDance. 
 In 2026, CATL became VNET’s largest shareholder and announced a deal to take a 49% stake in Zhongheng Electric’s controlling shareholder. It has since agreed with VNET to jointly develop gigawatt-scale datacenter campuses, and separately with Zhongheng to work on datacenter power systems. Between them, VNET covers the datacenter side, CATL leads green power and storage, and Zhongheng brings power conversion inside the hall. 
 CATL is also one of DeepSeek’s largest outside investors, which extends its reach downstream to the model layer. 
 Where Envision builds most of the pieces in-house, CATL links them through partnerships and equity stakes.
 China’s datacenter market is highly competitive. Rents have roughly halved over the past five years, to about $40/kW/month excluding power. Capex has fallen about 25% over the same period, to less than $3mm per MW. Power in Inner Mongolia costs about $0.055/kWh all-in, among the lowest in the world. 
 In a market like this, owning more of the value chain is one way to differentiate, a playbook familiar from China’s EV market, where players like BYD make much of what goes into their cars.
 It is too early to say whether vertical integration will become a meaningful advantage in China’s datacenter market. For now, it gives integrated players more control over cost and schedule, but hyperscalers still choose vendors mainly on resources and track record. That could change as power becomes harder to secure and the power system inside the datacenter is redesigned.
 Behind the paywall, we walk through how Galaxy was built and designed in detail. 
 On speed and cost, we follow Galaxy from land auction to customer acceptance and explain why capex keeps falling. 
 On power, we trace how China took a different path from the US, adopting 240V DC in its datacenters years ago, and walk through Galaxy’s live 5MW pilot. A larger version is planned for the next phase. 
 On cooling, we take apart a design common in northern China that offers one answer to the chiller debate in the US.

items.title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
items.content:
In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported.
 Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy .
 Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300.
 We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading.
 Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX.

 Source: Dwarkesh (Dylan’s Cousin) Podcast 
 Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity.
 Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result:
 Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang).
 GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss.
 Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy.
 Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by vLLM OSS ecosystem developer, Inferact.
 This was benchmarked on InferenceX/AgentX, the industry-standard inference benchmark supported by almost every major buyer of compute, from Microsoft Azure to Oracle to Meta and many more. Furthermore, it has the support of the ML community, including vLLM, LMCache, SGLang, PyTorch, and Huggingface, and the support of major labs like OpenAI, MiniMax, ZAI, Qwen, Moonshot Kimi, etc.
 Google potential TPU customers and current TPU customers are asking Google for AgentX results because of how realistic the AgentX benchmark is and how similar it is to their real inference workload. For our SemiAnalysis supply chain shipment estimates on TPUv8i, TPUv8t, TPUv9, TPUv10, check our Accelerator Model for full quarter by quarter breakdown of shipments. 

 Source: InferenceX 
 Star the InferenceX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful!. InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and soon, SambaNova and Trainium2/3.

 Source: InferenceX 
 Recommendation to Jensen NVIDIA only occasionally loses to AMD on some model/scenarios , but TPUs delivering better performance per dollar or competitive performance per dollar is a new experience that NVIDIA senior leadership is unwilling to accept. As soon as TPU posted its first AgentX result on Qwen3.5 397B FP8 showing that even TPUv7 FP8 could beat GB300 NVL72 FP4, NVIDIA tasked a strike force of human engineers and agent swarms to work 997, late into the night until 2am local time and on weekends, across USA and mainland China. Unfortunately for NVIDIA, their first GB300 FP4 counter submission is still 1.64x worse per dollar than TPUv7 FP8 for external customers across most of the curve. We do think that with enough agent swarms, NVIDIA could regain a slight performance lead on GB300 NVL72 FP4 vs TPUv7 FP8, but on NVIDIA FP8 versus TPUv7 FP8, we believe that it is not possible for NVIDIA to regain SOTA for certain models.
 One thing we hear a lot from open-source maintainers in PyTorch and NVIDIA customers is that there is a lot of bureaucracy; simple things, like adding a new feature to the NVIDIA driver to support a certain feature for PyTorch CudaGraph capture, have been stuck in “internal NVIDIA legal review” for three months. It makes little sense for lawyers to be the blocker for technical driver features. We have seen similar challenges when trying to get NVIDIA to add features like improving ConnectX, NVSwitch, HGX Board (Vulcan, Umbriel) DCGM power telemetry, where it takes a while just to get the timeline for the timeline. In comparison, startup mindset companies like AMD (under the leadership of Anush, Ramine, Vamsi, Lisa) can rapidly develop these features.
 There needs to be an cultural shift in massively reducing bureaucracy at NVIDIA. This is one of the biggest risks to NVIDIA Moat that Jensen has to tackle. In our experience and many customers experience, Nvidia is now slower moving than AMD, Google, and Amazon to external suggestion, git commits, and feedback. 
 That being said, certain teams at NVIDIA are cutting through the bureaucracy, such as the NVIDIA ex-CentML vLLM team . AMD and TPUs added innovative Megakernel decode support to open source popular production inference engine . Within a week, they were able to defend the NVIDIA by rapidly adding and merging Megakernel support too (PR approved by AMD vLLM maintainer). 
 TPU is making big headway into the ecosystem, and multiple models, like Day 0 Meta’s Muse Spark Open support and Kimi K3.1 Pro already has day 0 TPU support , as it applies the NVIDIA playbook of giving open-source maintainers lots of chips. In contrast, NVIDIA’s contribution of clusters to community maintainers has increasingly been wrapped in DMV style bureaucracy and stingy at best. For a $5 trillion company, one would expect NVIDIA to be more liberal in contributing resources to OSS developers who work for free on improving the NVIDIA stack. We hope Jensen figures out how to eliminate the bureaucracy slowing progress. 
 In comparison, AMD has been increasingly less stingy and providing the upstream vLLM, TileRT, SGLang, Tokenspeed, etc. maintainers liberal access to clusters and rapdily increasing the CI fleet without miminal levels of bureaucracy.

 Source: vLLM Dashboard 
 Meta’s Muse Spark Open FP4 816B on SGLang TorchTPU Agentic Inference Performance Meta is one of the early adopters of TPU and is already deploying TPUv7 in production using SGLang-TorchTPU.

 Source: Meta 
 Muse Spark Open is Meta’s latest 816B-parameter open model, and it is one of the launch models for SGLang-TorchTPU. On InferenceX’s agentic inference workload, a submission from RadixArk, a community developer and a lead maintainer of SGLang, shows that TPUv7 is competitive for decode performance per dollar even when using the cost basis of what Meta would pay when buying TPUs. For production inference, Meta uses SGLang for LLM inference and uses vLLM for RL training rollouts. When looking at end-to-end latency, TPUv7 still needs improvements to be competitive, such as continuing to optimize its prefill kernels. For decode kernels, TPUv7 SGLang is using a fully fused megakernel, which eliminates kernel launch latency. Furthermore, the submission uses SGLang HiCache CPU DRAM offloading using Google’s open-source, TPU native TPU-Sync library at high concurrency in order to improve prefix cache hit rates.

 Source: SemiAnalysis & RadixArk 
 Note that Muse Spark Open is an extremely GPU-optimized model, and, in theory, not friendly to TPUs at all. This is due to Muse Spark Open’s 64 head dim, which means that for long-context attention, 25% of the systolic array is padded.
 In comparison, GPU matrix cores consume small tiles, so a wide range of head dimensions, expert widths, and post-sharding KV head counts all land near peak. A dimension of 64 instead of 128 pays close to nothing on an H100 or a B200 and gets a cheaper attention layer for it. GPU architecture allowed researchers to prioritize evaluation performance without a loss in inference performance.
 This is quite interesting as TPUs can get quite competitive performance on a model that is extremely unfriendly to TPUs. Note that AI labs with lots of TPU capacity, such as Anthropic and Google Deepmind and soon OpenAI, typically co-design their models such that the attention shapes would fit nicely on TPUs to avoid this issue.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 When TPUs see model architecture with attention head_dim=256, they go full lambo mode.

 Source: Mario Kart 
 Great work to the RadixArk team on this amazing achievement! They are actively working on updating the documentation such that everyone can get access to this optimized SGLang Muse Spark Open TPU configuration. We expect more AgentX results from RadixArk soon, showing that its SGLang-TorchTPU stack is production-ready.
 GLM5.2 / 5.3 vLLM AgentX FP8 Agentic Inference Performance GLM-5.2/5.3 is a frontier open model. It is an MoE transformer with 744B parameters and roughly 39B active per token. The model supports a 1M-token context through DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): a lightweight indexer scores prior tokens, and full attention runs over only the 2,048 selected tokens for each query.
 For FP8, TPUv7 is the cheapest way to serve GLM-5.2 AgentX. From 60 to 300 tok/s/user, it delivers 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X at FP8 , and 4.4x that of H200 at 150 tok/s/user.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 FP4 GPUs Still Lead on Perf per Dollar Because GLM-5.3 was not natively QAT with block scale FP4, FP4 has a slight accuracy drop compared to FP8. FP4 GPUs still deliver more tokens per dollar at most speeds, as TPUv7 has no native FP4 support, and we will need to wait until Q1 2027 for TPUv8 with FP4 support, as tracked in our Accelerator & HBM Mode l. At 100 tok/s/user, GB300 and GB200 FP4 deliver 3.6x and 3.5x the tokens per dollar of TPUv7. FP4 halves the bytes per weight, and small batch decode is memory bound.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The SemiAnalysis AI Cloud & TCO Model provides a comprehensive breakdown of pricing across all accelerators currently on InferenceX, as well as many more, including future SKUs such as Nvidia Rubin Ultra and Feynman, AMD MI400 through MI700, Google TPU v8 through v12, and AWS Trainium3 through Trainium6.
 Get Access 
 GLM-5.3 Optimizations GLM-5.3 AgentX contexts reach 1M tokens with over 90% of each request already cached, so KV cache capacity sets how many users fit. There are four main changes:
 GLM-5.3’s attention reads one shared compressed KV entry per token, so splitting attention heads across devices would copy the whole cache to every device. Decode context parallelism (DCP) splits it by sequence position instead and merges partial attention results every layer.

 Source: SemiAnalysis & Google 
 Each query reads only the 2,048 cache entries an indexer selects. TPUv7’s SparseCores, built for scattered memory access, pick those entries and gather them while the TensorCore runs the attention math.
 TPUv7 uses registers that are 8 rows by 128 lanes. Data must be packed into them, which can fragment. The 128 indexer key bytes plus the scale byte add up to 129, one byte more than a 128-wide row, so the old layout rounded it up to 256. The new layout turns it sideways: tokens now run along each row, and each token’s key runs down 32 four-byte rows, plus one more row for the scale. That comes to 132 bytes, and only 3 of them are wasted.

 Source: SemiAnalysis & Google 
 One fused kernel runs routing; the experts, the all-reduce, and the attention merge become a single collective. TPU programs are compiled for fixed shapes, so Google added 4- and 8-token shapes for small decode steps, which had been padded to 16.
 Qwen3.5 397B AgentX Two weeks ago, Qwen3.5 397B became the first model Google submitted to AgentX. Its TPUv7 FP8 vLLM results on our agentic inference benchmark demonstrate that it is 1.67x better perf per dollar than even FP4 GB300 NVL72.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 NVIDIA may try to claim that it doesn’t care about the Qwen3.5 397B model, but from analyzing our upstream InferenceX submission analytics datalake, the reality is that NVIDIA has spent over 20% of the sweep GPU hours on Qwen3.5 for certain NVIDIA GPU SKUs so it is hard for NVIDIA to claim that. In addition, if you look at the NVIDIA engineers assigned to Qwen3.5, it is some of the top 10x inference performance engineers at NVIDIA in mainland China and USA, so clearly, NVIDIA cares about optimizing this model.
 Furthermore, certain major hyperscalers/AI lab use Qwen3.5 397B and multi trillion parameter scale up version based on Qwen3.5 397B architecture as proxy models when making hardware purchasing and capacity planning decisions. So, this is a very important model for certain token factories.
 For readers making purchasing decisions, our AI Cloud & TCO Model extends the analysis into cluster economics, including cash flow, investment returns, and accelerator residual values.
 Get Access 
 AgentX captures the four elements of an agentic workload:
 Multi-turn: a session includes many user / assistant interactions (tens or hundreds) compared to a handful in a chatbot scenario.
 Long context: system prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns make context accumulate quickly.
 High prefix reuse: since the conversation progresses linearly, where output from turn n-1 is concatenated to turn n
 Sub-agent bursts: a session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, which create bursty KVCache patterns.
 TPU was able to demonstrate that its upcoming TorchTPU vLLM stack can successfully handle agentic workloads.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 NVIDIA First Counter Submission NVIDIA engineers worked overtime to launch their counter submission FP4, which beats TPUv7 FP8 on decode performance, but there is a slight issue: they overtuned decode at the expense of prefill, hurting overall end-to-end performance. Thus, on end-to-end performance, TPUs FP8 is currently still beating GB300 NVL72 FP4.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Open Source Kubernetes llm-d puts TPUv7 far above GB300 FP8 for Decode Interactivity Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate hosts so long prefills do not stall generation. llm-d is the open-source K8s router that coordinates them, each host is 4 TPUv7 chips, and each result uses 24-32 chips.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Speed comes from capping how many requests each decode host runs, from one at a time at the low-latency end up to 112 at the high-throughput end. Requests over the cap wait for a free host, which adds to their TTFT. Even so, p90 time to first token at the fastest point is 8.6 seconds, against 11.1 for GB300 FP4’s fastest point.
 This uses llm-d, one of the largest ecosystem-based production inference kubernetes orchestrators. During the recent Kimi K3.1 Pro launch, they had Day 0 support for TPUv7 on llm-d .

 Source: InferenceX 
 At FP8, TPUv7 with llm-d beats GB300 at every interactivity, from >2x at high throughput to achieving more than 1000tok/s/user in the ultrafast region.
 Unfortunately, using this turn-based routing algorithm does lead to worse end-to-end performance for TPUs compared to GB300 TRTLLM FP4. However compared to FP8 and FP4 GB300 NVL72 SGLang, it is still much better.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Qwen3.5 TPU Optimizations Qwen3.5-397B mixes 45 linear attention layers, which keep a fixed-size state per request, with 15 full attention layers. Google describes three main changes:
 Decode megakernel. One kernel runs the whole decode step and prefetches the next layer’s weights while the current layer computes.
 Host DRAM offload. KV cache and linear attention state spill to host DRAM through TPU Sync, Google’s newly open-sourced offload framework.
 Cache-aware routing. llm-d sends each turn to the prefill host holding its prefix and keeps each session on its decode host unless that host is full. Google says routing to the exact data-parallel rank raised decode cache hit rates from 56% to 76%.
 Kimi K3 AgentX TPU from Inferact and AMD shipped megakernels for frontier MoE models first in open source engines. NVIDIA quickly followed within a week with its own megakernels.
 A conventional decode step launches hundreds to thousands of kernels, and the chip idles between them. A megakernel runs many layers in one long-running kernel that prefetches the next weights, while the current ones compute. AMD calls its version the MonoKernel. On GLM-5.2 across eight MI350X GPUs, AMD reports that it cuts a decode step from about 2,459 launches to 210 and runs 2.31x faster at batch 1.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 A megakernel removes the idle gaps between kernel launches. Read more about megakernels in our TileRT article:

 For this setup, DCP was used for prefill. The prefill and decode variants of context parallelism describe where each technique usually helps, not where it can run. K3 uses MLA which stores KV as one latent shared across heads, so TP cannot split it and every TP rank holds a full copy. DCP fixes this by giving each TP rank a different slice of tokens. Prefill context parallelism would have needed a lower TP degree, which copies weights onto more chips and leaves less HBM for the KV cache, already the scarce resource here.

 Source: Inferact 
 Competitive with GB300 FP4 at launch At launch on October 17, TPUv7 delivered 0.77x to 0.91x GB300’s tokens per dollar from 50 to 200 tok/s/user and was 1.6x faster for a single user, at 391 tok/s/user against 251. On Google’s internal cost it beat GB300 at 100 and 200 tok/s/user.

 Source: InferenceX 
 GB300 FP4 now leads by 1.5x to 2.6x after four NVIDIA refreshes. TPUv7 still delivers a competitive 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200 and B300, while VR200 delivers 4.3x to 5.6x TPUv7.

 Source: InferenceX 
 In an apples to bananas comparison between TPUv7 & Rubin NVL72, Rubin is up to 6x better perf per dollar. But note that this is an unfair comparison as Rubin should be compared to TPUv8i which we will be benchmarking very soon.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 It is important to note that Rubin’s results remain preview submissions . We look forward to NVIDIA providing direct Rubin access so we can independently reproduce these results and run the full InferenceX/AgentX suite.
 Built by the Ecosystem This result came from the vLLM ecosystem, not from Google alone. Inferact, founded by vLLM’s creators and maintainers, built the K3 megakernels with Google, and the two submitted the result together. The megakernel plugs into vLLM as a model runner that replaces only the forward, so vLLM’s scheduling, prefix caching and KV transfer work unchanged. The stack is open source on vLLM TorchTPU, and Inferact’s reproduction guide runs it from a Docker image. Ecosystem development like this has mostly happened on CUDA.

 Source: Inferact

items.title: Elon Is Doing It Again: SpaceX Will Be The World’s Biggest AI Cloud
items.content:
We wrote at length about how SpaceX’s plans for 10GW in 2027 was feasible , paving the way for 300b+ ARR. We received a lot of pushback from folks calling it impossible. Now, just two months later, we’re already seeing 3.6GW under construction across multiple sites, both existing and new . SpaceX has even revised its estimate up to ~13GW in 2027. This would be the largest amount of datacenter capacity ever built by any one company in that timeframe, roughly equivalent to all of Google’s datacenter capacity from 1999-2026 in just 1.5 years. We think it’s possible and have already identified >9GW of capacity. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 We’ve since written multiple update notes to our Datacenter Industry Model subscribers showing off all the sites that can make this possible. We now believe that SpaceX may be the fastest datacenter builder in the world , even more so than Chinese peers . Watch how Colossus 2 adds nearly two Stargate Abilenes (2GW) in just under one year!

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 These sites now build so fast that the power supply is often identified mid-flight. Looking at our Energy Model , we see that power under Elon’s management (>8GW) is less than our total datacenter power coming online (>9GW).

 Source: SemiAnalysis Energy Model 
 Datacenter Industry Model subscribers knew all of this before anyone else. On June 23, we sent our customers information on the infamous Elon “10GW in 2027” statement on SpaceX’s first earnings call by six weeks, pointing out a 5-10GW incremental order for 2027 was floating around the supply chain and that a new building was already under construction at Colossus 2, now publicly known as “MiniHard.” On September 14, before a single datahall went vertical, we identified >2GW of fresh sites , both at Colossus 2 and SpaceX’s Starbase campus.

 Starbase, Texas, October 29th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The Elon locations have a pioneering track record with us. We called Colossus 2 the first gigawatt datacenter in the world back in September 2025, when onsite gas was called a science experiment . We showed exactly how xAI bypassed the grid (and permitting!) with truck-mounted turbines, why the behind-the-meter playbook was going to spread to 40GW+ of behind-the-meter datacenters by 2028 , and how the Anthropic and Google deals turned SpaceX into the most profitable neocloud on earth . Now, Colossus 2 could soon house the largest BESS deployment in the world, with 5.9GWh already being installed, and more to come. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 This report unveils our analysis of SpaceX’s “proprietary plan.” From repurposing Starship’s rocket building and launching campuses into datacenter sites, to the gargantuan BESS deployment , buying out homeowners to house construction workers, and relocating mobile turbines, this report covers it all.
 For example, did you know TeraFab , Elon’s 100M sqft, 10GW+ chip fab project in Texas, will likely also have a datacenter? See the clip below of SpaceX representatives talking to Grimes County officials.

 Source: Local Filings
 Keep reading to find out why we think the TeraFab datacenter will be for third party renting!
 Subscribe now 
 And beyond the paywall, we dive deeper into the likely SpaceX power solutions, another site that may house a datacenter, and potential pricing for future SpaceX contracts, build off our proprietary SpaceX Funding Model as part of our Capital, Compute and Markets model. 
 Fastest Build Times In The World What does building two Stargate Abilenes in one year look like? Let’s talk about the Colossus expansions, where Elon is already trying to buy hundreds of nearby homes to both soothe noise complaints and provide construction worker housing . We’ve already spoken about MiniHard in Memphis finishing construction in just ~5 months, but the newly purchased “Gun Range” plot just south of the state line in Mississippi will take ~4 months!

 “Gun Range,” Colossus 2, October 28th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 To our knowledge, this would be the fastest greenfield datacenter ever built at scale. While most are fighting for 8-12-month build times, SpaceX has cut them in half.
 Looking closer at Colossus 2, we see SpaceX trying to break its own record again. SpaceX’s first retrofit at Colossus 1 took 122 days for 150MW, and Colossus 2 took just 91 days for 210MW. Now, SpaceX has taken the building (codenamed Project SPAM) directly in the middle of Colossus 2, and targets December to bring its first tranches online. With a construction start date of October 5, 2026, this could be shorter than the 91-day record, which itself broke the 122-day record; both are held by SpaceX.

 “Project SPAM,” Colossus 2, Mississippi, October 28th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model ; Note the Megapacks and Chillers already being deployed! 
 Colossus expansions were to be expected, but repurposing sites from Elon’s other ventures was not. For example, many are familiar with Elon’s Starbase in Texas, traditionally used for rocket building and launching. However, as flagged two months ago to Datacenter Industry Model subscribers , this site will now house two datacenters too!
 The site went from simply clearing ground at the end of August to full vertical construction by the end of September, and we now believe it will actively fit out datahalls in the coming weeks.

 Starbase, Texas, October 29th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 At this size, and with the knowledge of a 2027 timeline (meaning Vera Rubins), this site could be well over 1GW! Looking at the datacenter on the right, you can see that the steel mainframe is being built, while the roofing is actively following behind it. And on the left, you can see the transition from dirt to full preconstruction. These are multiple construction processes performed simultaneously, a visual representation of speed.
 Lastly, we have medium-high confidence that TeraFab will have a datacenter too. That’s right, the 10GW, 100M sq.ft chip fab venture from SpaceX will likely have a datacenter. We flagged this possibility ~3 months ago, and again 1.5 months, to Datacenter Industry Model subscribers, solely by examining preconstruction work and filings.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The project actually initially started as a datacenter and then quietly pivoted to TeraFab.

 Source: Local Filings 
 We showed the clip at the beginning (August 2026) of the site housing compute; furthermore, the representatives do not confirm that the datacenter will be for SpaceX’s use only, leaving room for third parties to rent the capacity too.

 Source: Local Filings
 The main remaining question is whether the current work on the ground is for one or more datacenters or for supporting facilities for TeraFab (like onsite gas, Central Utility Plant, etc.). We lean toward a datacenter for now, but suspect the vertical construction is moving slowly to ensure their JETI agreements/permits are fully compliant; otherwise, they may be subject to the TCEQ pauses or other regulatory scrutiny. Preconstruction work is so early that these pads can be pivoted a number of ways if datacenter work is not granted.

 TeraFab, October 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 How Are They Building So Fast? One thing often overlooked is that the Elon companies are some of the best hardware companies in the world. We mentioned in our previous newsletter that their labor can run at 3k workers per GW thanks to their top-tier engineers. However, we also believe that Tesla is manufacturing modular MEP equipment, allowing SpaceX to deploy so rapidly.
 If SpaceX and Tesla can manage their global supply chains appropriately, their partnership can easily construct GWs with far fewer constraints than others. This is like Crusoe manufacturing their own Switchgear to skip lead times , but on a massive scale. Tesla will likely become more than a BESS merchant to SpaceX soon.
 Largest USA BESS Deployment, Turbines, and A Grid Connection? Now that we’ve walked through GWs worth of sites, how will they power them? So far, we track 8GW+ of likely behind-the-meter capacity for SpaceX . This includes deals such as FTAI, Solaris, and others that only our Energy Model subscribers get access to. We have discussed how SpaceX decides the power on the fly, and one amazing example is the new Starbase, Texas site, where APRs are being deployed just one month after vertical construction started!

 Starbase, Texas, October 29, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The site may use >1GW of APRs, but judging by building size, this will not be enough. And looking at the (two!) pipelines underway, the site will likely have multiple GWs of power, and more turbines on the way. According to a TikTok with the Brownsville mayor, the site is building a fiber optic channel through the Port of Brownsville, as well as looking at leasing waterfront space (potentially for its own port). At such a massive scale, we suspect most of the temporary turbines from Colossus 2 will be relocated here.
 Next, let’s move on to Colossus 2, where the opposite is happening: a grid connection. According to TVA (the region’s utility), Macrohard (700MW) and MiniHard (450MW) have both requested service for their facilities. For now, we assume this grid connection services Macrohard and MiniHard in full.

 Source: Local Filings 
 We’ve already seen SpaceX building out the 500kV gas-insulated substation (GIS) to the left of MiniHard, which is scheduled to finish construction by December 31, 2026, and connect to the Freeport substation.

 SpaceX GIS Substation, October, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 This comes at the perfect time, as the turbines at the Southaven power plant must be shut down. The site can legally operate 2.7GW nameplate right now, but only 1.24GW nameplate by July 2027, due to the binding requirement signed July 30, 2026.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Energy Model , MDEQ 
 But the eagle-eyed reader may notice: after subtracting the ~1.2GW grid connection, we’re left with 1.3GW of compute… and 1.24GW of nameplate power generation… Recall, nameplate generation still takes a haircut on efficiency and derate , and IT MW doesn’t represent the full facility load . There could be a gap upwards of 300MW. How does this get solved?
 We think there are a few ways, and the Energy Model team will explore this power system in depth soon. But first: we think SpaceX has built the largest BESS field in the USA for a reason. With the BESS nearing 6GWh, we think the site will orchestrate gas and BESS to increase baseload, while the turbines cycle through charging them. If the datacenters are designed right (and our IT MW assumptions are correct), this could work. Given some clusters are customer-facing while others are for internal training, there could be an SLA uptime tiering to increase total capacity.

 Colossus 2, Mississippi, October 28th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 We suspect that with an ultralow PUE of ~1.10-1.15, variance in datacenter types (inference vs training, customer-facing vs internal usage), rack designs using less power (Project SPAM using half the fiber of others), and the oversized BESS, the project may still be able to cover a ~300MW shortfall.
 Beyond the paywall, we will further discuss the power situation, and how we think SpaceX economics could play out.

items.title: GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
