items.title: Datacenters 2027: The Year of Acceleration, +50GW in a Single Year
items.content:
Not a week goes without another piece of datacenter FUD. We’ve already debunked in depth why moratoriums aren’t as impactful as one may think . Despite that, many still misunderstand the pace of the global AI datacenter buildout. Just the other week, Brad Gerstner from Altimeter showed our data on the All-In Podcast and stated that “SemiAnalysis’ forecast of +43GW in 2027 is too aggressive” and that he thought only about 25GW would get built, close to half of our number, based on his “hunch”. But let’s not operate on hunches.
 It’s very tempting to cede to the FUD given all the constraints on the datacenter buildout: power, labor, supply chains, capital, and many more. But at SemiAnalysis, we care about the truth, not about narratives. And here’s the truth for you: one picture, >24GW of datacenters in advanced stage of construction, most of it to be delivered in 2027. Most of them are more than halfway done, with exterior cooling and electrical equipment already installed. That’s just 40 campuses, a tiny share of the multiple hundred sites in advanced stage of construction. We track them all, and for the full granularity, use our Datacenter Industry Model .

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 Of course, there are plenty of challenges and shortages. Behind these pictures, there are labor issues, supply chain delays, fundraising challenges, among many others. We’ve written in-depth about Modular Datacenters and Labor , Datacenter Electrical systems, Cooling systems, Behind-The-Meter power , the US Grid Constraints , and Nvidia’s ecosystem financial support . But the fact is simple: gigantic sites are simply getting built, and many are on time. For example, just go look at what Crusoe built in Abilene, what AWS built in Indiana, or QTS/Microsoft’s giant site in Georgia. These are the sites that have produced SOTA technology like GPT-6 and Fable 5.5. Looking ahead, despite all the constraints, an accelerating number of giant sites keep getting built, as shown by our Top 40 picture

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 If you ask any datacenter builder, they’ll tell you how hard it is, how some workers aren’t showing up, how vendors are delayed, and many other issues. All of this is accurate. And that’s why we’ve successfully called out countless datacenter delays and keep calling out developer timelines that appear overly aggressive in our Datacenter model, including the Oracle New Mexico Force Majure site delay in April . To be fair, +50GW is essentially the global cumulative datacenter market up through 2024 being built in one year! But our Datacenter Industry Model adjusts for all of that and still points to a material acceleration in datacenter capacity in 2027. So, what are we seeing that others can’t?

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 SemiAnalysis is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

 Let’s dig in. We’ll explore the following topics in this report:
 SemiAnalysis proprietary leading indicators: we’ll show a sneak peak of our proprietary data supporting our forecast, such as self-build construction starts and datacenter leasing (in MWs and USD). Year-to-date, slightly under USD 1T of binding / non-cancellable datacenter leases have been signed – that’s key to supporting our aggressive 2027-28 forecast.
 The shape of the buildout: how can we support +50GW in a single year? Where, what design, what power solutions?
 The “real” question: are we going to face a datacenter oversupply? As we explained in The Great Silicon Shortage , datacenters & power may be the tip of the iceberg, with memory and logic possibly becoming the new #1 constraint in 2027-28.
 Overall, we are very excited about 2027. The natural implication of the acceleration will be significantly more compute supply. That means cheaper and smarter AI, faster pace of AI model progress, and likely material revenue acceleration for leading AI labs and other token vendors. That also means unthinkable capex numbers. Reflexively rates will have to shoot up to enable the buildouts from a capital demand perspective. Let’s dive in!
 SemiAnalysis Datacenter Leading Indicators: how we see the buildout before everyone else Today we want to dive into two crucial indicators that give us strong confidence on our 2027 forecast. The first one is quarterly self-build construction starts. To accurately forecast US hyperscalers, we track the exact construction evolution of every single building. And the conclusion is simple: US hyperscalers have never launched more construction of datacenters. Each quarter, we track how many MWs start construction, and that number is going parabolic, driven in particular by two hyperscalers. If you want to know who or track the granularity of our data, subscribe to our Datacenter Industry Model. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The second indicator is Datacenter Leasing. We’ve talked about this a lot in prior reports, but as a quick recap: given the capital-intensity of building multi hundred MW datacenters, developers typically only spend 5-10% of project capital without a customer. They need a “pre-lease” to fund and develop the whole project. That’s typically a 15-20 year contract, with a TCV of $30-50B per GW. Check out our HPC Lease Tracker as part of the Datacenter Model to dive into actual contract economics.
 Subscribe now 
 As such, tracking these lease contracts is a key leading indicator, as it leads debt raises, which itself leads the actual buildout. A big reason why 2026 datacenter growth isn’t “that” high relative to 2025, is that quarterly datacenter leasing remained relatively stable between H2 2023 and H1 2025. Of course, the key reason was the Microsoft Datacenter Freeze, which we called out before anyone else in December 2024 for Datacenter model subscribers : the Redmond giant single-handedly drove the leasing market in 2023 and 2024, then paused, and others could only pick up what was left behind.
 Since H2 2025, things have dramatically changed. Oracle kicked off the era of gigantic leases, after closing on ~4.5GW of datacenter IT capacity across three sites between August and October 2025. Everyone else followed, and the pool of buyers has never been broader, with Meta, AWS, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, AMD, Anthropic and OpenAI all being in the market for GW-scale leases. There’s also a long tail of Neoclouds signing hundred-MW-scale deals.
 In USD terms, this means an unprecedented amount of lease value that builders can use to raise debt. Just in 2026 year-to-date, we’ve identified over a trillion USD of lease value that was signed and closed . That trillion is supporting a gigantic datacenter buildout in 2027-28. Our new Compute, Capital & Markets Model is now tracking all the debt raises and can confirm that most of this debt has been raised.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The shape of the buildout: how to build 50GW in a year Tracking all of these leading indicators has enabled us to forecast, before anyone else, the upcoming surge in orders for many industrial suppliers like Vertiv, ABB, Sterling Infrastructure. Check out our Industrials Model for in-depth coverage . However, the challenge is now going from orders to delivery. And resources have obviously become constrained, as power, labor, and sheer regulatory overhead are enormous burdens for developers. But the industry has promptly reacted with innovation.
 The first step is to simplify datacenter designs. We show below how Google has modularized their electrical architecture, removing a significant amount of outdoors cabling that requires onsite assembly, replacing them with prefabricated electrical modules. We track all the equipment changes (including suppliers) for datacenter designs and forecast orders in our Industrials Model 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials Model 
 Others have opted for more radical design changes. One example is Meta with its tent design, that we exclusively unveiled over a year ago . Another one is AWS which has materially simplified their shell design and launched a new rapid design dubbed “SAMDC”. Data halls are also increasingly prefabricated, an effort called Project Houdini at AWS. Construction timelines are now under 10 months. Hence our “ LEGO Datacenters ” title for the modular movement, you literally slot them in and go, and doing so allows for MEP labor (7-11 months of work) to drop up to 63%! We will have a full deep dive on the labor of the 2027 buildout coming soon.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials Model 
 In addition to hyperscale selfbuild, datacenter developers promoting prefabricated designs have also been remarkably successful. DayOne is likely the best example. With a total of ~3GW leased since their first deal in early 2023, the Singaporean company has been a rocket ship in terms of construction speed. While traditional developers have >18 months build timelines, DayOne cut this to ~9 months, which was key to signing huge deals with Firmus, OpenAI and Nvidia.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 Subscribe now 
 Another core issue is power, and again we think the issue is largely solved. We’ve been the first to talk about all issues on power, since March 2024 and subsequently given the grid headroom dips negative at the end of 2027 . This ended up driving AI Labs and hyperscalers to build their own power plants , better known as Behind-the-meter generation, bypassing 5-10year grid interconnection timelines. And while turbine incumbents like GEV quickly faced production bottlenecks, the industry quickly reacted and we’ve since seen a surge in new OEMs and new solutions supplying the market. From fuel cells to truck engines to refurbished turbines, the power generation problem has broadly been solved.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Energy Model 
 In addition, the buildout is now geographically diversifying. This naturally bypasses US labor, power, and (in some countries) permitting constraints. And as shown below, the ex-US buildout is sharply accelerating in 2027, and we expect it to gain a lot of market share in 2028, largely driven by US challenges.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model

items.title: ASML Is Building a Hybrid Bonding Tool!
items.content:
ASML has not announced anything yet, but its patent filings, a news report and its own roadmap all suggest so. We believe it will start with a die-to-wafer (D2W) hybrid bonding (HB) tool. This is harder to build than wafer-to-wafer but is where ASML could gain an edge. We see the move as a natural extension of ASML’s vertical integration, and one that should strengthen its customer ties.
 In this article we unpack the tool’s design end to end, starting with patent filings. What makes it unique is that it runs on a track . That changes how the tool and the dies move: each die rides its own holder past the process stations, and the tools get closer at each station to process the dies. The track’s independent shuttles also lift station utilization, save on duplicate tooling, and enable heterogeneous integration.
 We believe ASML could gain an edge in alignment accuracy and particle control for Hybrid Bonding. These are the two factors that set bonding yield. And ASML has expertise in solving the same problems in lithography.
 Despite the advantages, ASML still needs to solve challenges around feed-forward metrology, the die-to-wafer contact, the modification of the non-bonding tools so they can process dies on the track, and keeping the whole loop clean.
 We expect advanced logic, where D2W already runs in volume, to adopt ASML’s D2W HB tool first. This is bad news for Besi . Logic accounts for most of Besi’s HB business today concentrated at TSMC and Intel. ASML has been working with both for more than two decades and just announced a joint photomask initiative in September. We won’t be surprised to see a similar move in the back end process. Besi’s HBM prospects are also weakening. Korean challengers are catching up, in addition to an HBM adoption that we expect to slip to 2029 or beyond.
 ASML is Building a Hybrid Bonder We did a deep dive on hybrid bonding in 2024, and we still see it as the most transformative innovation in semiconductor manufacturing since EUV. Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) hybrid bonding (HB) is already in volume in image sensors and 3D NAND, and DRAM makers will be next. Die-to-wafer (D2W) HB is moving slower , because the industry still lacks mature tools that combine satisfying alignment accuracy and throughput (our check indicates upper bound in current applications is only one wafer per hour), which keeps cost per die high. Today D2W runs in volume only in logic: AMD has shipped hybrid-bonded V-Cache since 2022, and TSMC’s SoIC bonds at about 6um pitch today and targets 4.5um around 2029. The market expected HBM to become the big D2W volume driver from 2028. However, our view is different: we believe HBM will not adopt D2W HB before 2029 , if at all.
 Besi has led D2W and is the only supplier with tools in volume production. Everyone else is still trying to get a first tool qualified. But we believe the situation will soon change, because ASML is building a D2W hybrid bonding tool. Management hasn’t announced anything yet. But the company filed 27 bonding patent families between December 2022 and November 2024, most of them D2W, and the true count is likely higher because filings made after November 2024 are not yet public. The Elec also reported in March that ASML had started the architecture design of a hybrid bonder with Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG.
 In the anchor filing ( WO2025201788A1 ), ASML drew how its bonding flow works. Interestingly, the system looks nothing like a traditional D2W bonder (see Advanced Packaging Part 5 for how those work). Instead of a bond head picking each die off a diced wafer and placing it, ASML moves single dies on independent holders around a track (Fig 1). Each die passes inspection, cleaning, plasma activation and metrology (topography, leveling and alignment) stations before it reaches the bonding station where the chuck lifts the bottom wafer up to meet the die. We unpack the design in the sections below.
 Fig 1: ASML’s track-based D2W bonder, SA annotated and simplified 

 Source: ASML; SemiAnalysis Wafer Fabrication Equipment Model 
 ASML could be building a W2W hybrid bonding tool as well. According to a patent analysis by Inha University , ASML is likely building W2W HB equipment on its TWINSCAN platform, leaning on its wafer overlay accuracy. We focus on the D2W machine in this note, because it is the harder tool to build and the one where ASML could gain a real edge.
 …as Part of its Vertical Integration Initiative We believe this is a continuation of ASML’s effort to integrate vertically and tighten customer relationships. ASML bought Cymer for its light source in 2013, HMI for e-beam inspection in 2016 and Berliner Glas for optics modules in 2020. It shipped its first back-end product, the XT:260 i-line packaging scanner, in 3Q25. And most recently, ASML announced joint initiatives with TSMC , Intel Foundry and Samsung to move the industry from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks for High NA EUV.
 Building a bonder would be a natural next step. In fact, ASML’s own roadmap already puts bonding inside the front-end flow. Its 2024 Investor Day listed W2W and D2W hybrid bonding for NAND, DRAM and logic (Fig 2). And a July 2024 filing shows how the bonder and the scanner would work together by sharing die position data. Today a scanner printing on a bonded wafer must pre-align and coarse-align every die before it can expose. In ASML’s design the bonder already knows where it put each die and hands that map (a “coordinate system” in the filing) to the scanner, which checks a few marks and exposes. Customers get faster lithography on bonded wafers, and ASML gets to sell the bonder and the scanner as a pair.
 Fig 2: ASML’s map of front-end 3D integration 

 Source: ASML Investor Day, 14-Nov-2024 
 We expect advanced logic to be the first adopter. Logic is where D2W HB already runs in volume, and where the alignment requirement keeps tightening. TSMC calls overlay “always the biggest challenge” for SoIC. As its HB pitch moves from 6um to 4.5um by 2029, the placement accuracy requirement will tighten further. ASML is strong in alignment, as we will elaborate below, so an edge here should help it win logic customers first. Advanced logic dies are also among the most expensive chips, so logic customers can afford a premium tool. We expect ASML to price its tools at a premium to peers.
 In the next three sections, we discuss (1) the tool’s track system - the most unusual thing about it compared with what is on the market; (2) how ASML’s strengths in alignment, particle control and motion could make its HB tool superior; and (3) the challenges ASML or its supply chain partners still need to resolve to build a working tool. Let’s dive in.
 What’s Unique About the Tool One of the most interesting things about the tool is that it runs on a track . ASML names SuperTrak CONVEYANCE (Fig 3) as an example in its patent filing , so we assume it uses that track and we base our analysis on the track’s published design.
 The fundamental difference from a traditional bonder is where the die lives. In a Besi-type tool, the die is prepared elsewhere, and a bond head picks it up only for the final placement. In ASML’s design, each die sits on its own holder from the moment it leaves the carrier and stays there until the bonding step . The process stations are built around the track: the die stops in front of a station, the station cleans, activates or measures it in place, and the die moves on.
 Fig 3: SuperTrak CONVEYANCE track (HORIZON10 platform) 

 Source: Company website 
 Now let’s go through the process step by step . For illustration, we took the patent drawing and labelled every station in Fig 4. A gripper takes the die off its carrier and sets it on an empty substrate holder (206), which carries it along the track (202). The die stops in turn at the inspection, cleaning, plasma activation, topographic inspection, leveling, coarse alignment, position adjustment and fine alignment stations (210 to 226). At each stop the die stays on its holder, and the station does its work. Note the reversal here: in the patent it is the station’s sensor or head that moves in to reach the die, not the die that is carried into the tool as in today’s flow. After these steps the die arrives at the bonding station (228).
 This bonding station deserves a closer look . The first thing to note is that the final placement is done by the holder (206) and the chuck (234), not the track: SuperTrak’s spec sheet puts the shuttles’ repeatability at about 10um, nowhere near the 50nm placement accuracy the bond needs. Next, zoom in on the right-hand part of Fig 4 for the bonding work. The chuck lifts the bottom wafer to within tens of microns of the die, the holder’s actuators adjust the die’s position, the die is pressed onto the wafer to form the bond, and the holder releases it. The empty holder then starts another loop.
 Fig 4: Patent WO2025201788A1 Fig. 2 (left) and Fig. 6 side view (right), SA annotated 

 Source: ASML; SemiAnalysis Wafer Fabrication Equipment Model 
 This design has three major benefits:
 First, independent shuttles lift the utilization of every station . The number of stations per step can be set from that step’s cycle time: a three-second cleaning step gets three stations, and a 1.2-second bond step gets one, so every station stays busy. The patent asks for exactly this, to “occupy all process stations simultaneously”.
 Second, capacity is added by adding a station rather than a second tool, as long as the equipment chamber has room for it. That saves duplicate tooling and budget .
 Last but not least, the design suits heterogeneous integration : a new die type is a new software recipe, so mixed chiplets could share one line.
 That said, the track brings its own challenges around the non-bonding stations and the cleanliness of the whole loop. We come back to them later.
 How ASML May Gain an Edge Before that, let’s look at how ASML could bring its existing strengths to the HB tool.
 First, a reminder of why alignment accuracy and cleanliness matter so much in hybrid bonding. As we elaborated before , a single 1um particle between two full-thickness wafers can unbond an area around 10mm across , resulting in a defective bond (Fig 5). So particle control is extremely important for HB. Alignment matters for two reasons: placement accuracy sets bond yield directly, and alignment time weighs far more on D2W throughput than on W2W because it compounds with the die count. These two hurdles are what make hybrid bonding almost a front-end process.
 Fig 5: A small particle opens a void and an open contact in hybrid bonding 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 We believe ASML can tackle both with decades of experience solving the same two problems in lithography.
 For alignment, we believe ASML can reuse its wafer-alignment sensor technology. Based on its patent filings , the bonding system puts a tiny diffraction grating on each die and reads the die’s position from the light the grating scatters. The principle is the same as ORION , the wafer-alignment sensor on every new TWINSCAN since 2017. ORION was built to read marks that CMP and etch have tilted or deformed (Fig 6), and a mark on a bonding die goes through the same CMP and plasma activation as the copper pads next to it, so it carries the same asymmetry. We believe the same sensor family can serve the D2W bonder.
 Fig 6: A symmetric and a tilted alignment mark. Process steps shift the apparent center; ORION’s multi-color readout was built to see through that 

 Source: ASML, Aligning lithography to the nanometer, Dec-2021 
 Its sensing and motion capabilities also provide it with more room in total alignment error budget. Its NXT:2100i holds 0.9nm overlay on a single machine. And ASML can already measure the distortion of a W2W bonded wafer and correct the next lithography layer for it, bringing post-bond overlay from 40-60nm down to below 4nm (Fig 7). These are litho numbers, not bond results. But they mean ASML’s sensor and stage errors sit more than an order of magnitude below the 50nm a bonder needs. Higher stage precision leaves more room in a bonder’s error budget for the other factors: die shift on the holder, thermal drift and movement during contact.
 Fig 7: ASML metrology plus scanner correction brings post-bond overlay to 2.5-3.9nm 

 Source: ASML Investor Day, 14-Nov-2024 
 Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG are the likely component suppliers to help ASML’s bonder move fast on motion. Prodrive makes the linear motors and drives for ASML’s EUV maglev stages and has also built Hanwha Semitech’s SHB2 Nano bonder. VDL ETG builds ASML’s frames and modules (Fig 8).
 Fig 8: Prodrive’s linear motor (left) and VDL ETG’s wafer handler module (right) 

 Source: Company websites 
 On cleanliness, the requirements for ASML’s EUV systems are more strict as a bonder’s. Few tool makers have fought particles at the nanometer scale for as long as ASML. EUV scanners move reticles and wafers in vacuum and keep reticle particle adders at a level “ compatible with HVM requirements for sub-10nm node lithography ”. We believe ASML has thought about the bonding surfaces too: its bonding apparatus filing adds a tool that cleans the substrate supports and a sensor that watches their flatness, particle load and distortion.
 That said, contaminants in a bonder differ from those in a scanner. Most are dicing debris on die edges and particles landing on freshly activated, hydrophilic surfaces. We look for more detail on how ASML handles these bonder-specific contaminants in future filings.
 After the paywall we discuss the challenges ASML needs to tackle to build a working tool, and how its tool will impact on Besi’s business prospects.
 Open Questions ASML Needs to Solve
